title: Surveillance Blind Spot Mapping and Tradecraft: Navigating the Gaps in the Watched City
body:
The assumption that Meridian 88 is comprehensively surveilled is itself a product of surveillance—a carefully maintained perception that serves the interests of the corporate entities and municipal security contractors who benefit from behavioral compliance. In practice, the city's monitoring infrastructure is a patchwork of overlapping but inconsistent systems, maintained by competing vendors whose data formats are often mutually incompatible, and whose coverage maps contain thousands of dead zones resulting from budget disputes, hardware failures, and deliberate jurisdictional ambiguity at district boundaries. Professional intelligence operatives, and increasingly sophisticated independent actors, maintain living maps of these gaps and trade them as primary tradecraft currency.

Blind spot categories are informally classified into three types within the operational community. Hard gaps are physical spaces where no sensor infrastructure exists: the underside of the elevated rail viaducts along the old I-94 corridor through the Pilsen Remnant, the interior of the Calumet Wetland Reclamation Zone where wireless signal degrades beyond municipal sensor range, and the sub-basement levels of pre-Consolidation buildings whose owners never consented to infrastructure integration. Soft gaps are spaces where sensors exist but data is inconsistently processed—high-traffic transit interchange nodes where facial recognition systems are deliberately throttled to prevent processing bottlenecks, and areas where corporate surveillance jurisdictions abut without data-sharing agreements. Temporal gaps are periods when specific systems are offline for maintenance, calibration, or software update cycles, which occur on documented schedules that are theoretically internal but have leaked repeatedly.

The tradecraft of navigating blind spots has generated its own material culture within the intelligence community. Operatives in Meridian 88 use what practitioners call 'route threading'—planning movement paths that string together sequences of hard and soft gaps to create traversal corridors where continuous identity tracking is impossible. A well-threaded route from the Wicker Industrial Corridor to the Northwall lakefront can, according to experienced practitioners, reduce trackable exposure to under forty percent of total travel time. The route maps themselves are stored on air-gapped physical media—most commonly modified transit cards with expanded flash storage, chosen because transit cards are among the few physical objects whose possession is normalized across all citizenship tiers.

Municipal and corporate security agencies are aware of blind spot mapping as a practice and have developed countermeasures. The most effective is the deliberate introduction of false gaps: areas where visible sensor hardware is present but appears non-functional, while concealed backup sensors continue to operate. Several well-documented intelligence failures in the mid-2070s resulted from operatives trusting outdated blind spot maps that had been quietly patched. The result is an epistemological arms race in which the value of a blind spot map degrades rapidly over time, and the community of practitioners has developed verification protocols—small test movements by low-value couriers—to confirm gap status before committing high-value operations to a route.
headings: False Gap Operations and Verification Protocols
